Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, 4 October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A fundamental solution is normalized by its point source. For the Laplacian, a small enclosing flux determines that normalization. For complex diffusion, it is determined by a Gaussian mass limit and a continuously chosen matrix phase. The determinant's numerical value alone does not determine that phase.

The exact preceding proofs used here are Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1; Homogeneous extensions and angular moments, Theorem 6.1 and its angular foundations, A4–A5; the Schwartz Fourier foundations, F1–F5; Cauchy kernels and boundary limits, Corollary 2.2; Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, the polydisk proof and Lemma 3.1; and the compact approximation in Order, positivity and distributional limits. The finite algebra foundation, Sections 10.1–10.6, proves the determinant, inverse and orthogonal-basis operations. We prove the additional diagonalization, determinant differentiation and square-integral arguments below.

Choose the Gaussian phase from its matrix

We first supply the two finite matrix facts used in the construction.

Real symmetric diagonalization. A real symmetric matrix has a real orthonormal eigenbasis. Indeed, the continuous quadratic form has a maximum at some unit vector , by compactness of the real unit sphere. For , differentiate at the value of this form at . Its derivative is , which must vanish at a maximum. Thus is orthogonal to every , hence . Symmetry makes invariant: . Choose an orthonormal basis there by the finite Gram construction and repeat on this smaller symmetric matrix. Induction, starting at dimension one, proves the assertion. Positivity of is equivalent to positivity of all its eigenvalues by the resulting diagonal quadratic form. In particular a positive definite has a positive lower bound .

Determinant differentiation. If is differentiable and invertible, the finite multilinear determinant expansion gives To check the coefficient, write . Multilinearity gives : the identity permutation contributes the stated linear terms, while any nonidentity permutation uses at least two off-diagonal entries. Multiplicativity of the determinant then proves (M1). Determinants are finite polynomials and inverses are the adjugate divided by the determinant, as proved in the algebra foundation; in particular inversion is continuous and holomorphic wherever the determinant is nonzero.

Let be complex symmetric. Its entrywise real part equals its Hermitian part . For a complex vector , the real symmetric form satisfies . Hence positivity on real vectors is equivalent to Hermitian positivity on complex vectors. Set The cone is convex and open in the independent complex symmetric entries. Openness follows from the positive minimum of on the unit sphere and the elementary finite-coordinate bound for a small matrix perturbation. Every is invertible: would give , impossible for .

A bounded Fourier multiplier supplies the mass limit

Use the conventions proved in the Schwartz Fourier companion: The transform is a continuous automorphism of the Schwartz space, and its complex-linear transpose defines the transform on tempered distributions. In particular, bounded functions define tempered distributions, since Schwartz tests are integrable.

Theorem 3.1 (complex Gaussian transform and concentration). For and , the bounded smooth function has the tempered Fourier transform Its normalized pairing converges to as . This holds for Schwartz tests and for every compact test with integer . Uniformly in and , In particular, every even integer is allowed.

Proof of the transform. Start with and real positive definite . The orthogonal diagonalization proved above reduces the Fourier integral to the product of scalar Gaussian integrals. The real linear substitution has absolute determinant one, by the affine integration theorem included with U011. The scalar formula is proved with its exact mass in the Fourier companion, F3: The product yields (3.2) with .

For fixed real , both sides are holomorphic in the independent symmetric entries on . On a compact subset of this cone, compactness of its product with the real unit sphere gives one with . Each matrix-entry derivative of the integrand is a polynomial in times that integrand. A polynomial times is integrable, by the scalar Gaussian estimates in F3 and Fubini. Dominated difference quotients therefore give joint continuity and coordinate holomorphy, hence full holomorphy by U015's polydisk proof. The branch and rational inverse give it for the right side too.

Equality on the real positive definite matrices suffices here. Around a fixed such matrix, choose a small complex polydisk inside whose real coordinate cube consists of positive definite matrices. Hold all but the first entry real, and use the one-variable identity principle on the real interval of that first entry. Repeat coordinate by coordinate, now allowing the previously treated entries to be complex. Equality follows throughout the polydisk. U015, Lemma 3.1, then extends it across the connected cone. The substitution , with Jacobian , proves the formula for every .

For a boundary matrix take . Since , the original exponential has modulus at most one; dominated convergence against each Schwartz test gives its tempered limit. Formula (2.5) gives the same bound for the transformed exponential. The constants and the inverse matrices converge, so the transformed expressions also converge against each Schwartz test. The Fourier transpose is continuous for this convergence, by F5. Passing to the limit proves (3.2) for every .

Changing to and using evenness gives (3.5), including its sign and factor. Its multiplier has modulus at most one by (2.5), and tends pointwise to one as . Since , dominated convergence and inversion at zero prove the concentration for Schwartz tests, including compact smooth ones.

The weight is integrable when . Indeed U018's polar formula reduces the tail to a constant times ; on the unit ball the weight is bounded. Cauchy–Schwarz gives For the second inequality expand The Fourier derivative identity and the preceding square-integral formula identify each weighted square integral with . For compact tests, the U008 approximation has a common compact support and converges in every derivative through order . On that support it also converges in the norms in (3.4). The estimate makes the normalized pairings converge uniformly over and as the smooth approximations converge. At each fixed , their ordinary integrals in (3.3) converge to the displayed integral by uniform convergence on that compact support. Passing the uniform estimate, then using the smooth concentration limit and a three-term difference estimate, proves both (3.4) and the mass limit for the test.

There is no need for the real and imaginary parts to commute. For example Its determinant is , and the displayed real parts are semidefinite. Purely imaginary invertible matrices are included for the same reason.
